evidence: The race is real - sessionPidUnder walks with sequential ps calls and signals a bare pid - but both remedies the reviewer proposed cost more than the exposure: a `ps -o comm=` check reintroduces the compiled-binary-name matching that the code's own comment records as drifting every release, and a start-time compare narrows rather than closes a POSIX signal-by-pid race. Exposure is bounded: same-uid SIGTERM in the few ms between the last ps read and process.kill, with request.json already written so a mis-signal costs a nuisance, not the switch.
guidance_note: Record an accepted failure mode in the comment beside the code that accepts it, so a reviewer reads the decision instead of rediscovering the gap and spending a round on it.

evidence: The PR deletes hooks/injector/ entirely while laws-excise.js's file header still described 'Part B = an injected self-resume', so the header named a component with no implementation left anywhere in the repo; the same hunk had already corrected the equivalent claim 100 lines lower, which makes the header a straightforward miss rather than a judgment call.
guidance_note: When a PR deletes a mechanism, grep the whole file - header and module docstrings included - for prose naming it, not only the block being edited.

evidence: `catch (_e) { return 0; }` genuinely collapsed 'ps ran and the pid is gone' with 'ps could not run at all', so a missing procps would surface as the walk's misleading 'could not find the claude session'. The agent took neither suggested remedy (error text in the eventual die, or an up-front `command -v ps`) and instead discriminated on the throw's shape - a numeric `.status` means ps ran - which is a sharper cut than either.
guidance_note: Before writing a catch that maps an external command's failure onto a domain value, enumerate every failure shape that command can produce - spawn failure, nonzero exit, timeout, invocation it does not support - and decide each one, because a partial enumeration is what the next review round finds.

evidence: I reproduced the exact shape on bash 5.3.9: a script file whose last statement is `bash child.sh` forks (child pid 86105, ppid 86103 = launcher), while `bash -c 'echo ...; bash child.sh'` does exec-collapse (child pid == launcher pid). The reviewer's premise - that the script-file tail collapses the way the tool-shell `-c` string does - is false, and the agent's stated mechanism (a script is parsed incrementally so the shell cannot know the command is last) explains why.
guidance_note: A test comment that explains one shell workaround invites the reviewer to assume the neighbouring case needs the same one; say in the comment which case does not collapse and why, not only which case does.

evidence: laws-switch has three distinct exits on the new resolution path (match, LAWS_LAUNCHER_PID unset, pid set but not on the ancestry) and section 8 exercised only two; the third is reachable in production when the launcher dies and the orphaned session still carries the env var. The agent's fix used a live background sleep rather than a dummy number, which is a strictly stronger fixture.
guidance_note: When adding a resolution path, enumerate its exits and give each one a case before review - the missing branch here was the one the happy-path test could never reach.

evidence: Reading the merged walk at bb4498f, `if (parent === launcher) return cur;` runs before `if (parent <= 1) return 0;`, so with launcher==1 the not-found arm is unreachable and sessionPidUnder(1) always returns the topmost non-init ancestor - meaning a stale LAWS_LAUNCHER_PID=1 would SIGTERM the user's login shell rather than fail loudly, which is the agent's point and the opposite of the reviewer's 'handles launcher==1 correctly'. The pid-1-ENTRYPOINT deployment the reviewer invokes is speculative and nothing in this repo ships claude-laws that way.
guidance_note: The ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag is a false positive here: the `launcherPid <= 1` guard appears verbatim in the round-0 diff hunks for F1 and F3, so 63670fe did not introduce it.

evidence: execFileSync had no timeout and sessionPidUnder can call it 256 times, so one stuck ps hangs the command with no diagnostic - a silent shape in the same function the previous round had just hardened against silent shapes. The agent's own words name the causation: 'a hang was the one remaining silent shape after the ENOENT fix', and the ETIMEDOUT throw carries no numeric status so it lands in the die arm F3's fix had just built.
guidance_note: When the fix for a swallowing catch is 'distinguish the real failure from the legitimate one', write the whole failure-shape table for that call in the first pass; F3's fix enumerated two shapes and left two, and each remainder cost a round.

evidence: F3's fix made 'numeric .status' mean 'pid gone, top of chain', but a BusyBox-style ps that rejects `-o ppid= -p` also exits nonzero with a numeric status, so an unsupported invocation was laundered into 'top of chain' at the first hop. The reviewer's stderr discriminator is sound and the agent verified it (a genuinely gone pid exits nonzero with empty stderr on macOS ps and procps), and the merged code at bb4498f reads `if (typeof err.status === 'number' && !stderr) return 0;`.
guidance_note: The agent's own note that its first usage-error fixture was vacuous - execFileSync forwards child stderr to the parent, so matching the complaint anywhere passed even under a swallow-mutation - is the reusable move: assert the complaint appears inside the die message, not merely somewhere in stderr.

narrative: Eight findings across three rounds on a PR replacing a Bun-inspector session-exit with a SIGTERM ancestry walk. The agent pushed back three times and was right all three times - I reproduced the bash fork-vs-exec measurement behind F4 myself, and the merged walk at bb4498f confirms the pid-1 argument behind F6. The one avoidable round is round 2: it exists because F3's fix enumerated only two of the four ways `ps` can fail, and rounds 1 and 2 then delivered the missing two (F7 timeout, F8 unsupported-invocation) one at a time. Note the merge was later force-reverted off master per ticket promptctl-injector-xy0.4, so none of this code shipped.
guidance_observations: Three of eight findings were pushbacks and all three held up under independent checking, which is evidence the pushback discipline in address-pr-reviews is calibrated rather than reflexive here.
The agent measured before pushing back (two bash versions for F4, real ps behavior for F8's discriminator) rather than arguing from first principles - that is what made the pushbacks checkable.
Every accepted fix in this PR names a mutation check that kills the new assertion, which is why none of the fixes here produced a follow-on finding of its own.

evidence: The new law stakes its value on being countable ('this one has a number... Count before you claim') and then ships a RIGHT example that is three lines (a type plus a two-line comment) against a two-line before-state, so the worked example contradicts the claim it exists to demonstrate. I confirmed against `gh pr diff 29` that the merged SKILL.md still carries the comment ending 'the pass ends smaller than it started', so nothing was changed.
guidance_note: When a law's selling point is that it is checkable, run its own check on its own worked example before shipping it - counting the RIGHT block would have caught this in the authoring pass.

evidence: 'that law's repair rule' sat next to a [LAW:comments-carry-meaning] citation while the rule belonged to polishing-by-subtraction, so a reader would look the rule up in the wrong section. The merged text reads '**A wrong comment is fixed by shrinking it.** [LAW:polishing-by-subtraction]', but that landed incidentally in commit b23ff97 - a revert whose message says the pointed-at rule 'no longer exists' - with no reply ever posted on the thread.
guidance_note: A skill that borrows another skill's vocabulary should cite the token, never a deictic ('that law', 'the rule above'), because the referent moves the first time either file is edited.

evidence: Deleting the law count left the README sentence 'unfold into the rest' with no antecedent, and the parallel edit in SKILL.md kept a noun ('unfold ... into laws that all say') - so the same de-numbering pass produced a broken sentence in one file and a correct one in the other. `gh pr diff 29` confirms the merged README still says 'unfold into the rest'.
guidance_note: When deleting a fact that appears in several files, read each edited sentence end-to-end afterwards; the sibling edit here shows the agent knew the right shape and just did not apply it twice.

evidence: The new guidance states a checkable edge ('the replacement is shorter than what it replaced') and two lines later offers a GOOD fix of 44 characters replacing a 28-character wrong comment, which fails its own check; the merged file still contains both. This is normative guidance other agents execute literally, so a self-contradicting example is worse here than in ordinary prose.
guidance_note: Apply a rule you are writing to the examples in the same block before shipping - or state the exception (a replacement carrying a fact absent from the code may be longer) rather than leaving the reader to reconcile them.

evidence: Trigger-level `paths-ignore` produces no workflow run and therefore no check for the head SHA, which the repo itself later confirmed in PR #30's config comment: 'Filtering at the trigger creates no workflow run at all, and /address-pr-reviews polls the head SHA for one'. The thread was never answered because the PR merged at 01:07:17, six minutes before this round was posted.
guidance_note: Do not merge a PR seconds after pushing a commit the reviewer has not seen; the trigger change here shipped unreviewed and had to be reverted wholesale in a follow-up PR.

evidence: The workflow file's own header says it is generated by agent-code-review-setup/install.sh and that the installer overwrites local edits, so a hand-added paths-ignore would vanish on the next install - and the agent's own commit message for a97dec7 admits this ('re-running that installer will overwrite this edit') while shipping it anyway. PR #30 then moved the change into .github/code-review.conf, which is the installer's per-repo input, confirming the reviewer's premise exactly.
guidance_note: When a file states in its own header that it is generated, editing it is never the fix; find the generator's per-repo input first - the agent already knew this, wrote it in the commit message, and edited the copy regardless.

evidence: The comment justified `**.md` over `**/*.md` by claiming the latter 'requires a literal / and so misses root-level files like README.md', but globstar in GitHub's path filters consumes zero path segments, so `**/*.md` does match a root-level README.md; the chosen pattern is harmless, the stated reason is false. The comment was never corrected - PR #30 deleted the whole block along with the filter.
guidance_note: A comment asserting a tool's matching semantics is a testable claim; check it against the tool's documented table before writing it down, since the reviewer will and the round costs more than the check.

evidence: Same premise as F5 restated by a second review scope: a path-filtered-out run reports no status at all, so a required check stays 'Expected - waiting for status' on a markdown-only PR. Confirmed correct by the repo's own decision in PR #30 to use an exclude that still registers and completes a run rather than a trigger filter.
guidance_note: Four of this round's six findings are duplicates of two claims from different review scopes; the process cost here is that no reply was posted to any of them, not that the reviewer repeated itself.

evidence: Duplicate of F6's premise from a second scope, and equally right: the generated workflow's header names install.sh as its source of truth, and the hand-added block would be silently dropped on the next reconvergence. PR #30 relocated the exclusion to .github/code-review.conf.

Third restatement of the required-check risk, with the sharpest illustration: this very doc-only PR would not have triggered a review under its own new rule. The repo accepted the premise in PR #30 by dropping the trigger filter entirely.

narrative: A documentation PR that added the polishing-by-subtraction law, and the only PR in this batch where the agent never replied to a single thread. Round 0's four findings (F1-F4) were all correct and all merged unaddressed except F2, which was fixed incidentally by an unrelated revert. Then, forty seconds after pushing a97dec7 - an unrelated CI change adding trigger-level paths-ignore to a file whose own header says it is generated - the agent merged, and round 2 landed six findings on that commit post-merge. All six were right: the change was reverted and relocated in PR #30 the next day, which is round 2 paid for twice.
guidance_observations: The rule 'reply on every thread' was not followed at all here; nine of ten findings have no reply, and three correct findings shipped to master because of it.
Merging while a review round is in flight converts findings into follow-up PRs - PR #30 exists only because a97dec7 merged unreviewed.

The agent's own commit message for a97dec7 records the exact defect the reviewer then found ('re-running that installer will overwrite this edit'), so this round was avoidable by heeding a fact the agent had already written down.

This PR authored guidance about not growing comments during review while itself shipping two worked examples that fail their own stated check - the authoring pass needs the same countable check the law demands of code.

evidence: The comment's rationale ('The laws ARE the markdown here') does not cover PROVIDER_CONTRACT.md, which states the contract action_provider.py must satisfy and sits beside it, so a blanket `*.md` exclude would have withheld exactly the drift a reviewer should catch. The agent scoped the exclude to three prose-only trees and, notably, verified the result against the action's own matcher (src/diff.js filterFiles) rather than by reading the globs.
guidance_note: Before writing an exclusion whose justification is a claim about a whole file class, enumerate the files the class actually contains - the claim was refuted by a single counterexample already in the repo.

evidence: The comment restated '300s' while REGISTER_TIMEOUT_S = 300 in action_provider.py owns that number, so the comment was a second copy with no mechanism to catch drift; the merged conf file now says 'waits out its registration timeout' with no value. Small and uncontested.
guidance_note: A comment that quotes a constant's current value duplicates a fact that has an owner; name the constant or the behavior instead.

evidence: F1's fix widened the exclusion from one blanket pattern to three named trees but left the sentence above it reading 'Both trees named below', so the fix's own comment contradicted the fix's own list - a whole review round for one word. The merged file reads 'The trees named below', and the agent dropped the count rather than correcting it to three so it cannot disagree again.
guidance_note: After changing the arity of a list, re-read the prose that introduces it - a fix that edits a value and leaves its neighbouring sentence is the single most common cause of a second round in this batch.

narrative: The follow-up that undid PR #29's trigger-level paths-ignore, moving the exclusion into .github/code-review.conf where the installer reads it. Both round-0 findings were correct and cleanly accepted, and the F1 fix was verified against the review action's real matcher rather than by inspection - the strongest verification practice in this batch. Round 1 exists for one reason: the F1 fix changed one pattern into three and left the word 'Both' in the sentence above the list. That is the cheapest possible avoidable round and the clearest instance of the pattern this audit hunts.
guidance_observations: The agent verified its fix by running the consuming matcher over the real file tree (16 prose files excluded, 11 markdown still reviewed, no source file excluded) instead of reasoning about globs - that verification is why F1 did not recur.
The one avoidable round was a comment describing the pre-fix state; a diff-local read of the changed hunk plus its surrounding prose would have caught it.
Choosing to delete the count rather than correct it is the right repair shape - a fact that is not stated cannot drift - and it matches the law this repo had just written.

evidence: stop() asked 'was the launcher the most recent tool call' when the question it needs answered is 'did the close-out run', so the documented, instructed order (commit, push, then close out) plus one confirming git call produced a spurious block and a message telling the agent the handoff may be lost when it was not. The fix deleted last_tool_call rather than adding a case, which is a genuine net simplification.
guidance_note: Write the predicate as the question the caller actually needs answered; 'was it the last call' was a proxy for 'did it run', and the proxy is what broke.

evidence: Matching git by basename does admit any file named git, and the reviewer's primary remedy (shutil.which plus 'is it a real git binary') would refuse a fully-qualified /usr/bin/git on a machine whose PATH names the Homebrew git - a false denial on ordinary machines to close an adversarial hole. The agent took the reviewer's own stated fallback: restore the scope sentence to the module docstring and pin the behavior with a test, so the boundary is a recorded decision rather than an oversight.
guidance_note: When a gate's threat model excludes an attacker, state that boundary in the module docstring and pin it with a test at authoring time - the agent had deleted exactly that sentence in a comment-stripping pass, which is what made the gap read as an accident.

evidence: One subprocess.run call bypassed the run() helper and so inherited the real environment, contradicting the isolation invariant stated eleven lines above it; because resolve_ceiling() runs at import, a developer's own ~/.claude ceiling file could decide the outcome. The test suite lying about its own isolation is worse than the case it was testing.
guidance_note: When a test file states an isolation invariant in a comment, that invariant needs an enforcing helper every case routes through, not a comment - a single raw subprocess call is enough to void it.

evidence: The gap was real - `push` was in the allowlist with no flag inspection, so `git push --force` was permitted while the comment promised the gate protected committed work - but the fix chosen (per-subcommand flag allowlists) is the decision that produced F7, F9, F11 and F14 and was deleted wholesale three rounds later, after which the agent recorded `push --force` as knowingly permitted. In hindsight the right answer was to fix the overpromising comment and refuse to build an argument grammar.
guidance_note: Before building a grammar over an unbounded external argument surface, decide whether the threat model justifies it: the correct split answer here was 'the comment overpromises, and inspecting git's arguments is not something this gate should attempt' - accepting the fix instead cost three rounds and was reverted.

evidence: os.path.realpath never performs a PATH search, so a bare-name `finalize-session` invocation resolved against the hook's cwd and a genuine close-out was classified as neither permitted nor launched. shutil.which applied only when the token has no path separator resolves it the way the shell would while the realpath identity comparison still runs afterwards, so an impostor on PATH is still refused - this fix survived to the merge unlike the git-argument work.
guidance_note: When comparing a program token against a known file, resolve the token the way the shell that will run it does; realpath answers a different question than PATH lookup and silently disagrees only for bare names.

evidence: The agent states it outright: 'this one is a regression I introduced. Widening closed_out from was-the-launcher-the-last-call to did-it-ever-run fixed the spurious-block bug and bought this in exchange.' With the tmux transport compacting in place, one ancient launcher success in the same transcript would have waved through every later breach, defeating the gate. The turn boundary is the right scope and keeps the case the widening was for.
guidance_note: When widening a predicate's scope to fix a false negative, name the new scope's upper bound in the same change - going from 'the last call' straight to 'anywhere in the session' skipped the only bound that was correct.

evidence: F4's fix filtered only `-`-prefixed tokens, so `git push origin +main:main` and `git push origin :topic` passed vacuously - and the reviewer correctly notes the agent had itself named `+refspec` syntax one round earlier as a reason a flag blocklist could not work, then shipped an allowlist with the same hole. The operand-shape fix that followed was itself deleted two rounds later, so patching again was the wrong direction even though the premise was right.
guidance_note: When you name a class of inputs as the reason to reject one design, write the accept/reject table for that class before shipping the replacement - the agent knew about +refspec and still shipped a check that ignored it.

evidence: permitted() checked only same_file(program, LAUNCHER) and never the arguments, so the launcher's undocumented internal modes - --iterm-worker, which kills a caller-supplied pid, and --detached-worker, which interpolates a caller-supplied CLAUDE_BIN into a tmux command string - were reachable through the gate with one Bash call and no setup. This is the strongest finding in the batch and needed no pre-planting, unlike the git-by-name gap the agent had just accepted as out of scope.
guidance_note: The ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag is a false positive for causation: the launcher branch read `return same_file(program, LAUNCHER)` in the round-0 diff hunks too, so 0ba989b did not introduce this. The reusable move is to read the callee's own argument parser before deciding a program is safe to permit by identity.

evidence: `git commit -am msg` was permitted before F4's fix (the round-0 check was `statement[1] in NONDESTRUCTIVE_GIT`) and denied after it, so the hardening broke a routine close-out idiom - a false denial in a gate whose whole purpose is to force the close-out through. The bundling rule the agent added to restore it then introduced F14's vacuous all() and was deleted one round later.
guidance_note: A false denial in a gate that exists to force one action is worse than the permission it withholds; when a hardening pass starts refusing the workflow it protects, that is the signal to remove the check rather than to add a rule for the idiom it broke.

evidence: `git -C <dir> status` was denied because arguments[0] was read as the subcommand, and the `cd <dir> && git ...` workaround was denied too since every chained statement must be permitted - so the gate could make committing outstanding work impossible while its denial message promised git still worked. The agent posted a plan to consume global options, then publicly retracted it and deleted the entire git argument grammar instead, which is the correct fix and the right moment to stop.
guidance_note: The ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag overstates causation: the round-0 check `statement[1] in NONDESTRUCTIVE_GIT` denied `git -C dir status` too, so this predates fb3302b. The reusable move is the agent's own: when four of five findings in a round are your own checks refusing legitimate work, delete the checks instead of extending them.

evidence: F4's fix classified every `-`-prefixed word as a candidate flag with no notion of role, so `git commit -m '-1 experiment'` - one shell word after quoting, and a message shape the instruction explicitly asks the agent to produce - was denied; before that fix only the subcommand was read, so it worked. The agent retracted its 'fix positionally with arities' plan in the same round and deleted the grammar, which resolves this without a parser.
guidance_note: A checker that classifies words independently of position will misread a value as a flag; if you are not willing to write the real grammar, do not write the half of it that inspects arguments at all.

evidence: The mechanics are as described - permitted_launcher advanced index past the end of the list and the trailing slice check then passed vacuously, so `--goal` with no value and `--reset badvalue` were classified CLOSEOUT - but the reviewer itself says 'not exploitable', and the whole cost is one wasted allowance on a call the launcher rejects with exit 2 immediately and loudly. Duplicating the launcher's own `case clear|compact` guard in the gate would be a second copy free to drift.
guidance_note: When a fix walks an option list by arity, decide what happens when the list runs out before writing the loop; the vacuous-pass shape here is the same one F14 found in permitted_flag, in code written the same afternoon.

evidence: F8's fix refused any remaining `--`-prefixed word, but finalize-session recognises its worker modes only as $1 and folds everything after the --goal/--reset walk into AGENT_MESSAGE verbatim, so a legitimate handoff message beginning with `--` was denied at PreToolUse and, worse, uncredited at Stop. Reading the launcher's actual case statement let both this and F8 be satisfied at once rather than traded off.
guidance_note: Mirror the callee's own parser rather than inventing a stricter one: the refuse-unknown-`--`-by-default rule looked safer than naming three flags and was in fact wrong, because it refused input the callee accepts.

evidence: F9's bundling rule made a bare `-` permitted for any subcommand, because `word[1:]` is empty and `all()` over zero elements is True - a textbook vacuous quantifier opening a hole in a default-reject allowlist that had rejected `-` before the rule existed. The deletion of the whole grammar removes the function and the bug with it.
guidance_note: An `all()` over a derived sequence needs its empty case decided explicitly; this is the second vacuous-pass bug in the same file in the same round (see F12), which makes it a pattern rather than a slip.

evidence: diff, log and show inherit git's `--output=<path>`, so a subcommand classified as read-only was an arbitrary-file-write primitive past a gate that correctly denies Write and Edit - qualitatively different from the accepted force-push trade-off because it writes outside the repo. The narrow reject on -o/--output for those three subcommands closes it without reopening the flag-allowlist design.
guidance_note: The ON-POST-REVIEW-COMMIT flag is a false positive for causation: the prior grammar also let reading subcommands 'take any flags', so --output was permitted before the deletion too. The reusable move is to check whether a subcommand you are calling read-only can write - 'reading destroys nothing' was an assumption, not a fact about git.

evidence: The any()/all() asymmetry is real, but the exploit needs a denied compound call to be credited, and closed_out() filters on the tool_result's is_error before launched() is consulted - so above the ceiling classify()'s all() has already passed for anything that ran, and below it any() is the right question. The reviewer conceded it could not confirm the is_error mechanism it depends on, so the premise is a live hypothesis rather than a demonstrated bug.
guidance_note: The reviewer's general instinct - two code paths answering 'is this the launcher' should answer it identically - was vindicated one round later by F20 on a different path, so a pushback on one instance is worth pairing with a sweep of the others.

evidence: run()'s default ceiling_file called tempfile.mkdtemp() per invocation across roughly eighty calls and never removed any of them, while the transcript and log tempfiles in the same function were unlinked - so the cleanup discipline was applied inconsistently within one helper. One shared scratch root cleaned via atexit is the right shape.
guidance_note: The ON-POST-REVIEW-COMMIT flag is a false positive for causation: the per-call mkdtemp is original-PR code in run(), not something a fix introduced. The reusable move is that a test helper creating temporary state owns its teardown for every resource it creates, not for the two that were easiest.

evidence: On F13 the agent wrote 'a test now greps the launcher for its --*-worker) case arms and asserts the gate's set matches, so a fourth entry point added later fails the suite' - and the reviewer found that no such test exists, so WORKER_MODES remained a hand-copied duplicate with nothing forcing it to track the launcher. A promised test that was not written is the cheapest possible avoidable round.
guidance_note: Anything promised in a plan reply is part of the fix; before replying 'Fixed in <sha>', re-read your own plan and confirm every element of it is in the commit.

evidence: launched() treated any statements() ValueError as 'did not run' while classify() already had the lenient reaching_for_launcher fallback for exactly that case, so a genuine close-out invoked with double-quoted expansion - legal per finalize-session's own documented contract and unrestricted below the ceiling - would be uncredited at a later Stop in the same turn. The asymmetry between the two parse paths is the defect, not the strictness of statements().
guidance_note: When one caller of a parser has a fallback for parse failure and another does not, that difference is a decision that has to be stated or removed; here it was neither.

evidence: The agent concedes it: 'this is a real regression from my previous round's launched() fallback'. F19's fix routed launched() through reaching_for_launcher, which checks only same_file and lacks the WORKER_MODES exclusion is_launcher carries, so a worker-mode invocation with unparseable quoting would be credited as a completed close-out - reopening exactly the hole F8 was raised to close.
guidance_note: When adding a fallback path for a predicate, call the predicate rather than re-deriving a looser version of it; the fallback here rebuilt half of is_launcher and lost the half that mattered.

evidence: The PR replaced the 'a payload with no transcript_path fails loudly' case with a missing-hook_event_name case rather than adding it, so a real loud-failure input lost its only coverage. The removal is visible in the round-0 diff hunk quoted under F3, before any fix commit, so this is a defect in the original PR that took four rounds to be noticed.
guidance_note: The ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag is a false positive for causation - the test swap predates every fix commit. When a rewrite changes what a test asserts, treat the old assertion as coverage to be re-homed rather than replaced.

narrative: Twenty-one findings over six rounds on a PreToolUse gate for the context ceiling, and the most instructive PR in this batch. Nine of the twenty-one exist because of an earlier fix on the same PR, and eight of those nine trace to two decisions: accepting F4 by building a git argument grammar, and F8's refuse-unknown-`--`-by-default launcher check. The agent eventually diagnosed the loop itself - in round 2 it publicly retracted three plans it had just posted and deleted the whole git grammar, recording `push --force` as knowingly permitted, on the grounds that four of that round's five findings were its own checks refusing legitimate close-out work. That reversal was correct and is the single best judgment call in the batch; it just arrived two rounds after the evidence for it did. Rounds 2 and 4 are avoidable: round 2's five findings are all downstream of round-1 fixes, and round 4's F20 is a self-described regression from round 3's fix.
guidance_observations: The dominant cost here is not missed bugs but self-inflicted false denials: a gate whose purpose is to force one action was repeatedly patched into refusing that action, and each patch cost a round.

The agent posted plan replies before implementing and then had to retract three of them in one round - the retraction was honest and public, but the plans were committed to before the round's findings were read as a set.

Reading the callee's own parser (finalize-session's `case ${1:-}`) resolved two findings that had looked like a trade-off, and the reverse - inventing a stricter grammar than the callee's - caused F13; that asymmetry is the clearest reusable lesson on this PR.
A test promised in a plan reply (F13) and not written became F18 a round later, which argues for verifying the commit against your own plan text before replying 'Fixed in <sha>'.
Two vacuous-quantifier bugs (F12, F14) appeared in code written the same afternoon, both of the form 'a loop or all() that passes when its sequence is empty'.
